sections.title: The hook
sections.intro_md:
On 21 September 2025 an ambulance left Guwahati airport carrying the body of a singer. The 30 km drive to his home normally takes an hour. It took about seven, because lakhs of people walked beside it, singing his songs. Zubeen Garg had drowned in Singapore two days earlier, and Assam stopped.

That is a useful first picture of the state: a place where a song can still move a city, and where identity is felt in the body. Assam is a long green valley cut by one of the largest rivers on Earth. It grows about half of India's tea, holds about four in five of the world's greater one-horned rhinos, and wraps visitors in a hand-woven cotton towel called a gamosa. It has the oldest working oil refinery in Asia and, from 2026, a chip plant. It also carries one of India's hardest questions: who belongs here? Today you meet Assam through things you can see and hear: golden silk, a monk's dance, a burial mound, a pepper that once held a world record.

sections.title: Where you are
sections.intro_md:
Assam sits in India's north-east, joined to the rest of the country by the Siliguri Corridor, a strip of land about 22 km wide at its narrowest. It touches Bhutan and Bangladesh and seven Indian states: Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Manipur, Mizoram, Tripura, Meghalaya and West Bengal.

Think of three pieces. The **Brahmaputra Valley** is the long heart, running about 700 km from Sadiya in the east to Dhubri in the west. The **Barak Valley** in the south (Silchar, Karimganj, Hailakandi) is Bengali-speaking and drains a different river. Between them sit the **hills**: Karbi Anglong and Dima Hasao, home to Karbi and Dimasa people and run by autonomous councils.

The capital is Dispur, a district of Guwahati. The state has 35 districts since January 2024. In 2011 it had 3.12 crore people, about the population of Malaysia, on 78,438 km², a little smaller than Panama. It used to be bigger. Nagaland (1963), Meghalaya (1972), Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh were all carved out of colonial Assam.

sections.title: The river and the land
sections.intro_md:
Everything in Assam answers to the Brahmaputra. The river enters from Arunachal Pradesh, braids across a plain 80 to 90 km wide, and leaves for Bangladesh. In the monsoon it can spread several kilometres from bank to bank, dropping silt that makes the valley fertile and floods that make it dangerous. The Rashtriya Barh Ayog counted about 40% of Assam's land as flood-prone, against roughly 10% for India as a whole.

Rain feeds it from both sides: the Himalaya to the north, the Meghalaya plateau to the south. The river is also restless. It moves its channels, eats villages on one bank and builds sandbars (chars, or chapori) on the other. Some of the most interesting places in Assam are these in-between lands: an island the size of a city, a hill town where birds fall out of the night sky, and a forest one man planted on a sandbar.

spotlights.name: The Brahmaputra
spotlights.spot_it: A river so wide in the rains you cannot see the far bank, with sandbars, ferries and fishing boats mid-stream.
spotlights.story_md: Most big Indian rivers carry female names. This one is a son: Brahmaputra, son of Brahma. In Tibet it is the Yarlung Tsangpo; in Bangladesh it becomes the Jamuna. In Assam it is so wide that for centuries it had no bridge at all. The first, the Saraighat bridge at Guwahati, opened only in 1962. The river carries one of the heaviest silt loads of any river in the world, and drops it as it slows on the plain. That is why it braids into dozens of channels and why its islands appear and vanish within a lifetime. Assamese songs call it Luit, and Bhupen Hazarika's most famous song is addressed to it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It made the valley's soil, its floods, its trade routes and much of its poetry.
spotlights.memory_hook: A male river with a female temper: it gives soil and takes villages in the same season.

spotlights.name: Majuli, the shrinking island
spotlights.spot_it: Flat green island of paddy, wetlands and bamboo villages, reached only by ferry from Nimati Ghat near Jorhat.
spotlights.story_md: Majuli is a river island big enough to be a district, India's first island district since 2016. Guinness recognised it as the largest river island in 2016. It is also disappearing. Early 20th-century records put it at roughly 1,250 km²; recent satellite studies give figures from under 500 to about 880 km², depending on the year and what counts as island. A 2025 EGU study counted 107 of 210 cadastral villages lost to erosion in 70 years. Majuli is the home of the Vaishnava satras (monasteries), of mask-makers, and of Mising villages on stilts. When people say Assamese culture has a capital, they often mean this island.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Assam's religious and artistic heartland, and a live case study in river erosion.
spotlights.memory_hook: The island that houses Assam's monks is being eaten by the river one village at a time.

spotlights.name: Jatinga, where birds fall from the night
spotlights.when: September and October, moonless foggy nights
spotlights.spot_it: A small ridge village with watchtowers and lamps; the event itself happens in the dark, on misty nights after 6 pm.
spotlights.story_md: On a few foggy, moonless autumn nights, birds fly towards the lights of Jatinga and crash or land dazed. For decades the story was that birds came here to commit suicide. That is a myth. A five-year study in the Indian Forester found about 50 of the 200-plus local species involved, eight of them making up 75% of the birds, mostly young ones. The explanation: night-flying birds disoriented by fog and wind steer for the brightest light, which villagers once lit to catch them. Hunting is now discouraged, and in 2017 the district banned strong lights during the season.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A famous 'mystery' that turned out to be birds, weather and lamps.
spotlights.memory_hook: Not bird suicide: bird confusion, plus a man with a lantern.

spotlights.name: Jadav Payeng, the Forest Man
spotlights.spot_it: A slight man in a gamosa among tall trees on a sandbar in the Brahmaputra.
spotlights.story_md: In 1979, after floods left dead snakes baking on a bare sandbar, a Mising teenager named Jadav Payeng started planting bamboo there. He kept going for decades, tree by tree, on Aruna Chapori near Jorhat. The result, called Molai forest after his nickname, is usually given as about 550 hectares, larger than New York's Central Park. Elephants, deer, rhinos and tigers have been recorded passing through. Forest officials only found out about it in 2008, when they followed a herd of elephants. He received the Padma Shri in 2015.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A one-man answer to erosion, on the river that causes it.
spotlights.memory_hook: One boy, one bamboo shoot, forty years: a forest bigger than Central Park.

sections.title: Rhinos, gibbons and a pig the size of a cat
sections.intro_md:
Assam is one of the richest wildlife states in Asia because it sits where the Indian, Himalayan and Indo-Burmese worlds meet, and because its floodplain grasslands, now rare elsewhere, survive here. It has seven national parks. Two of them, Kaziranga and Manas, are UNESCO World Heritage Sites, both inscribed in 1985.

The headline animal is the greater one-horned rhinoceros. In the early 1900s perhaps a couple of dozen survived in Kaziranga. Assam now holds about 3,260, about 80% of the world's total, and in 2025 recorded no known rhino poaching. Around the rhino is a cast of rarer creatures: India's only ape, a monkey named after the man who described it, a river dolphin that is nearly blind, and the smallest wild pig in the world.

spotlights.name: Greater one-horned rhino in Kaziranga
spotlights.spot_it: A grey armoured rhino in tall elephant grass or a pool, skin folded like riveted plates, a single thick horn.
spotlights.story_md: Kaziranga's protection story often starts with a disappointed tourist. Mary Curzon, wife of the Viceroy, visited around 1904 or 1905 and saw only hoofprints. She is said to have pressed her husband to act, and the area was made a reserve forest in 1908. The 2022 census counted 2,613 rhinos in the park. Kaziranga also holds wild water buffalo, swamp deer and one of the densest tiger populations anywhere. Every monsoon the Brahmaputra floods it, and animals climb artificial highlands or cross National Highway 715, where speed limits are enforced for them.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The world's main stronghold of the species, rebuilt from near zero.
spotlights.memory_hook: A Vicereine who saw no rhinos started the park that now holds two-thirds of them.

spotlights.name: Manas National Park
spotlights.spot_it: A clear blue-green river leaving the Bhutan foothills, grassland on one bank, forest on the other.
spotlights.story_md: Manas sits at the foot of the Himalaya, where the Manas river leaves Bhutan. It joins Bhutan's Royal Manas park across the border. During the Bodo insurgency of the late 1980s and 1990s, poaching wiped out its rhinos and UNESCO put it on the List of World Heritage in Danger in 1992. After the Bodoland agreement of 2003, rhinos were moved back in from Kaziranga and Pobitora from 2006, and the park left the danger list in 2011. It is one of the last homes of the pygmy hog, the hispid hare and the Bengal florican.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A park that was lost to conflict and recovered.
spotlights.memory_hook: Manas lost every rhino in a war and borrowed them back from Kaziranga.

spotlights.name: Gee's golden langur
spotlights.spot_it: A long-tailed monkey with cream to deep gold fur and a black face, often in high branches.
spotlights.story_md: This monkey is found only in a small patch of western Assam and neighbouring Bhutan. It was brought to scientific notice in the 1950s by the tea planter and naturalist E. P. Gee, and named Trachypithecus geei after him. Its coat changes with season and age, from creamy white to deep gold. It is endangered, split into fragments of forest by farms and roads. Some live on Umananda, a tiny island in the Brahmaputra at Guwahati, where they were introduced.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One of the rarest primates in India, found almost nowhere else.
spotlights.memory_hook: A tea planter's name, a golden coat, and a range smaller than one district.

spotlights.name: Hoolock gibbon
spotlights.spot_it: Tailless ape swinging arm over arm through the canopy; males black with white brows, females buff. Heard before seen.
spotlights.story_md: India has exactly one kind of ape, and Assam is its best home. Hoolock gibbons have no tail and move by brachiation, swinging hand over hand through the canopy. Pairs sing loud duets at dawn that carry for more than a kilometre. Males are black with white eyebrows; females are a pale buff. The Hollongapar Gibbon Sanctuary near Jorhat, a forest island among tea gardens, is the easiest place to hear them. A railway line cuts straight through it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: India's only ape, and a test of whether tea country can keep its forest.
spotlights.memory_hook: The only ape in India sings a duet at dawn in a tea garden forest.

spotlights.name: Ganges river dolphin
spotlights.spot_it: A grey back and long thin beak breaking the brown surface for a second, then gone. Locals call it xihu.
spotlights.story_md: The river dolphin of the Brahmaputra lives in water so muddy that sight is almost useless, and its tiny eyes lack a lens. It hunts by echolocation, clicking and listening. It surfaces every minute or two to breathe, with a sound that gives it its Assamese name, xihu (shihu). Guwahati adopted it as its city animal, and India made it the national aquatic animal in 2009. Dams, fishing nets and sand mining are its main threats.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A near-blind mammal that tells you how healthy the river is.
spotlights.memory_hook: A dolphin with no lens in its eyes, seeing the river with sound.

spotlights.name: Pygmy hog
spotlights.spot_it: A tiny dark brown pig, about 25 cm high, with a short tail, in tall grass.
spotlights.story_md: The smallest wild pig in the world stands about 25 cm at the shoulder and weighs 6 to 10 kg. It was thought extinct until it was found again in Assam in 1971. It needs tall wet grassland, the same habitat people burn and graze. Since 1996 a breeding programme near Guwahati run with Durrell Wildlife Conservation Trust has bred hogs and released more than 150 into protected grasslands. The pygmy hog-sucking louse, a parasite that lives only on it, is just as rare.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A flagship for the grasslands Assam's rhinos also depend on.
spotlights.memory_hook: The world's smallest pig came back from 'extinct' in Assam.

sections.title: People by numbers
sections.intro_md:
The 2011 census counted 31,205,576 people in Assam, at 398 per km², above the national average. About 86% lived in villages. The sex ratio was 958 women per 1,000 men and literacy 72.2%.

Religion is where Assam differs most from India. Hindus were 61.5% and Muslims 34.2%, the second-highest Muslim share of any state after Jammu and Kashmir. Christians were 3.7%, mostly in the hills and among tea-garden communities. Muslims in Assam are themselves two groups: Assamese-speaking indigenous Muslims (Goria, Moria, Deshi and others) and Bengal-origin Muslims who settled mostly after 1900. That distinction matters in Assamese politics.

Assam is also home to many peoples: Bodo, Mising, Karbi, Dimasa, Rabha, Tiwa, Tai Ahom, Sonowal Kachari, the tea-garden Adivasi brought from central India in the 1800s, and Bengali Hindus. No census since 2011 has been published, so these numbers are 15 years old.

sections.title: Kamarupa to the Ahoms
sections.intro_md:
Assam's written history begins as **Kamarupa**, a kingdom named in an Allahabad pillar inscription of the 4th century. Its best-known king, Bhaskaravarman, hosted the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang around 640 CE. Later dynasties, the Mlechchhas and the Palas of Kamarupa, left copper-plate land grants and temples such as the carved, earthquake-wrecked ruins of Madan Kamdev near Guwahati.

In 1228 a Tai prince named Sukaphaa crossed the Patkai hills from the upper Burma border with a few thousand followers. His dynasty, the **Ahoms**, ruled for almost 600 years, longer than the Mughals, the Marathas or the British lasted in India. They absorbed local peoples, adopted Hinduism over time, kept court chronicles called buranjis, and fought off repeated Mughal invasions. The word 'Assam' itself is probably linked to the name Ahom. The kingdom collapsed under civil war and three Burmese invasions from 1817, and the British took it by the Treaty of Yandabo in 1826.

spotlights.name: Sukaphaa, the first Ahom king
spotlights.spot_it: Statue of a crowned king with a sword at the Sukaphaa memorial at Jorhat; his day is celebrated on 2 December.
spotlights.story_md: Sukaphaa was a prince of Mong Mao, a Tai state on today's China and Myanmar border. In 1228 he crossed the Patkai range with followers, horses and elephants, and settled in the upper Brahmaputra valley. He founded his capital at Charaideo around 1253. Instead of wiping out local people, he married into and allied with Morans and Borahis, a pattern that let a small Tai group rule a mixed population. Assam marks 2 December as Sukaphaa Divas, or Asom Divas.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Founder of the state that gave Assam its name and its long independence.
spotlights.memory_hook: A Tai prince walked over the Patkai and started a 600-year kingdom.

spotlights.name: Charaideo Moidams
spotlights.spot_it: Grassy, rounded hillocks rising from flat land, each with a small octagonal brick shrine (chow chali) on top.
spotlights.story_md: The Ahom kings were not cremated. They were buried in vaulted chambers under artificial mounds called moidams, with clothes, weapons, ivory and, in early centuries, attendants. Charaideo, the first capital, holds about 90 of them. UNESCO inscribed the site in July 2024, India's 43rd World Heritage Site and the first cultural one in the north-east. Many were robbed long ago: by the Mughal general Mir Jumla's army in 1662 and later by British-era diggers. Press reports nicknamed them Assam's pyramids.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A royal burial landscape unlike anything else in India.
spotlights.memory_hook: Kings under hills: Assam buried its rulers in mounds, not ashes.

spotlights.name: Lachit Borphukan and the Battle of Saraighat
spotlights.spot_it: Bronze statue of a commander in mid-stride with a raised sword, on the river at Guwahati.
spotlights.story_md: In 1671 a large Mughal fleet under Raja Ram Singh came up the Brahmaputra to take Guwahati. The Ahom commander Lachit Borphukan, sick with fever, had himself carried to the river and led the counter-attack. The Ahoms used the narrow stretch at Saraighat to trap the bigger boats and won. A famous story says he executed his own maternal uncle for slacking on a defence wall, saying 'my uncle is not greater than my country'; it comes from later tradition. Since 1999 the best cadet at India's National Defence Academy receives the Lachit Borphukan gold medal.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The battle that kept Assam out of the Mughal empire.
spotlights.memory_hook: A feverish general on a boat stopped the Mughal navy at Saraighat.

spotlights.name: Rang Ghar
spotlights.spot_it: Two-storey brick pavilion with a curved roof shaped like an upturned royal boat, crocodile carvings at the ends.
spotlights.story_md: The Ahom kings watched buffalo fights, elephant fights and Bihu dances from this pavilion on the Rupahi field. Rang Ghar was built in brick around 1746, replacing a bamboo one. The mortar is famous: lime mixed, by tradition, with sticky rice, duck eggs and black gram. It is often called Asia's oldest surviving amphitheatre, a claim that is better treated as local pride than a checked fact. Its boat-shaped roof is now used everywhere as a shorthand for Assam, on signboards, logos and wedding cards.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The most recognisable Ahom building, and a symbol of Assamese identity.
spotlights.memory_hook: A royal grandstand held together with rice and eggs.

compare.difference: Talatal Ghar is the palace complex nearby, with storeys going down into the ground; Rang Ghar is a single viewing pavilion.

sections.title: Tea, migration and the question of who belongs
sections.intro_md:
British Assam was built for tea. From the 1840s planters cleared forest and brought indentured labourers from Chota Nagpur, Odisha and Bengal, many of whom died on the journey or in the gardens. Their descendants, the tea-garden Adivasi, are now millions strong. The British also encouraged Bengali Muslim peasants to farm the riverine chars and brought Bengali Hindu clerks for the offices. Bengali was even made the language of courts and schools from 1836 to 1873.

Out of this came Assam's central anxiety: fear that the Assamese would become a minority in their own land. It shaped the language riots of 1960 and 1961, the six-year Assam Movement from 1979, the Assam Accord of 1985, the National Register of Citizens in 2019 and the protests against the Citizenship Amendment Act that December. The same years also brought violence: the Nellie massacre of 18 February 1983 killed about 2,000 Bengali-origin Muslims in one morning by official count, and far more by other estimates, and insurgent groups such as ULFA fought the state from 1979.

spotlights.name: Gopinath Bordoloi
spotlights.spot_it: Portrait of a man in white khadi with round spectacles; his name is on Guwahati's airport.
spotlights.story_md: In 1946 the British Cabinet Mission plan would have grouped Assam with Bengal in one provincial section, where Muslim League-led Bengal would have had the majority. Gopinath Bordoloi, then Assam's premier, refused, and persuaded Gandhi to back him. Many in Assam believe this kept the province in India. He was the state's first chief minister after independence and died in office in 1950. He was given the Bharat Ratna in 1999, and Guwahati's airport carries his name.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The leader credited with keeping Assam out of the plan that could have taken it to Pakistan.
spotlights.memory_hook: Bordoloi said no to grouping, and Assam stayed in India.

spotlights.name: The Assam Movement and the Assam Accord
spotlights.spot_it: Black-and-white crowds of students marching with banners in Guwahati; today, the Swahid Smarak memorial to the movement's 855 dead at Boragaon.
spotlights.story_md: It began in 1979 when a by-election in Mangaldoi revealed a sharp rise in voters, many alleged to be from Bangladesh. Students of the All Assam Students' Union led six years of strikes, oil blockades and civil disobedience. The Assam Accord, signed on 15 August 1985 with Rajiv Gandhi's government, set 24 March 1971 as the cut-off: those who came after it would be detected and expelled. The student leaders formed a party, Asom Gana Parishad, and won the state election months later. Prafulla Kumar Mahanta became chief minister at 33.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The cut-off date in this accord still decides citizenship debates in Assam.
spotlights.memory_hook: Students shut down a state for six years and came out as its government.

spotlights.name: The National Register of Citizens, 2019
spotlights.spot_it: Queues of people outside NRC Seva Kendras clutching folders of documents: land deeds, voter rolls, school certificates.
spotlights.story_md: To apply the 1985 accord, the Supreme Court ordered Assam to update its 1951 citizens' register. About 3.3 crore people applied and had to prove that they or their ancestors were in Assam before 24 March 1971. The final list, published on 31 August 2019, left out 19,06,657 people. It pleased almost no one: Assamese groups said too few were excluded, while families found that one sibling was in and another was out. Six years on, the list has not been formally notified, and people left out still go before Foreigners Tribunals case by case.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The largest citizenship-verification exercise in Indian history.
spotlights.memory_hook: 3.3 crore applicants, one cut-off date, 19 lakh left out.

sections.title: Assamese, Bodo and a script on bark
sections.intro_md:
Assamese (Axomiya) is the easternmost of the Indo-Aryan languages, a cousin of Bengali and Odia. In 2011 it was the mother tongue of 48.4% of the state, with Bengali at 28.9%, Hindi 6.7% and Bodo 4.5%. Assam has three official languages: Assamese, Bodo in the Bodoland region, and Bengali in the Barak Valley.

You can hear Assamese before you understand it. Where Hindi has an 's', Assamese often has a soft throat sound, written x: Assam is *Axom*, Sankardev is *Xonkordeu*. In script it shares most letters with Bengali but has its own ৰ (ra) and ৱ (wa). In October 2024 the central government declared it a classical language, along with Bengali, Marathi, Pali and Prakrit.

Language has been a battlefield here. In 1960 the Assam assembly made Assamese the sole official language; on 19 May 1961 police fired on Bengali protesters at Silchar station and 11 died, a date still marked as Bhasha Shahid Divas. Bodo, written in Roman and Bengali-Assamese script before, switched to Devanagari in 1975 after its own movement and entered the Eighth Schedule in 2003.

spotlights.name: Sanchipat manuscripts
spotlights.spot_it: Long, narrow cream-coloured pages with Assamese script and painted miniatures in red, yellow and green, stacked between wooden boards.
spotlights.story_md: Before paper, Assam wrote on bark. Scribes stripped the inner bark of the agar tree (xasi, Aquilaria), cut it into strips, rubbed it with mustard oil and dried it until it was smooth and tough. Ink came from silkworm excreta, cow urine and plant dyes. On these sanchipat pages the satras copied Sankardev's Bhagavata and the Ahom court wrote its buranji chronicles, and painters filled them with miniature scenes. Some survive in the satras of Majuli and Barpeta and in museum collections. The same agar tree is today valued for agarwood oil, among the most expensive raw materials used in perfume.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The material record of Assamese literature and history.
spotlights.memory_hook: Assam's books grew on a tree that now sells for perfume.

sections.title: A monk's reformation and a goddess on a hill
sections.intro_md:
Two very different religious worlds sit side by side in Assam. One is Shakta and Tantric, centred on the goddess Kamakhya, with animal sacrifice, secret rites and one of the most important pilgrim sites in India. The other is the reforming Vaishnavism of Srimanta Sankardev, which from the 15th century rejected idols, sacrifice and much of caste ritual in favour of chanting God's name.

Sankardev's movement, Ekasarana Dharma, built two institutions that still shape every Assamese village: the **satra**, a monastery, and the **namghar**, a prayer hall that doubles as village meeting place. Its art forms, from Sattriya dance to borgeet songs and Ankiya Naat plays, are now classical arts.

Islam arrived early too. A Turkic general, Bakhtiyar Khalji, crossed into Kamarupa around 1206, and an Assamese Muslim tradition grew up that sings in Assamese. At Hajo, a Hindu temple, a mosque and a Buddhist legend share one hill town.

spotlights.name: Srimanta Sankardev
spotlights.spot_it: Painted portrait of an old man with a white beard, seated, with a manuscript; often shown with his disciple Madhavdev.
spotlights.story_md: Sankardev was a scholar, poet, playwright, composer, painter and social reformer in one life, which tradition says lasted 119 years. He taught that devotion to Krishna through hearing and chanting his name was enough, without idols, sacrifice or Brahmin gatekeeping. He accepted disciples from tribal and Muslim backgrounds, including a Garo, Govinda, and a Muslim tailor, Chandsai. He wrote some 240 borgeet songs, of which only 34 survived a fire, and in about 1468 staged Chihna Yatra, a play with painted scenery that Assamese tradition counts among the earliest open-air theatre productions anywhere in India.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The single most important figure in Assamese culture.
spotlights.memory_hook: One man wrote Assam's songs, plays, dance and religion, and lived to 119 if you believe the dates.

spotlights.name: Satra, the Vaishnava monastery
spotlights.spot_it: A long thatched or tin-roofed prayer hall facing a central courtyard, with rows of monks' quarters (hati) around it.
spotlights.story_md: A satra is a monastery and an arts school. Monks called bhakats live around a central prayer hall, and some satras, like Auniati, Kamalabari, Garamur and Dakhinpat on Majuli, keep celibate monks who enter as boys. Here they learn Sattriya dance, the khol drum, borgeet singing and mask-making. The head, the satradhikar, can be a powerful figure. Majuli once had about 65 satras; erosion and migration have left about 22. Barpeta Satra in lower Assam is the other great centre and runs itself through an elected committee.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The institution that kept Assamese performing arts alive for 500 years.
spotlights.memory_hook: A monastery where the monks rehearse as hard as they pray.

spotlights.name: Namghar, the village prayer hall
spotlights.spot_it: A long hall with a sloping roof and open sides; inside, no idol, only a wooden throne-like stand holding a scripture.
spotlights.story_md: In most Assamese villages the namghar is the centre of life. It has no idol. At the far end sits the guru asana or thapana, a tiered wooden seat that holds the Bhagavata. People gather for nam-prasanga (group singing), for village meetings and to settle disputes, and plays are staged here at night. Historians often describe it as an early village parliament, open to people who would have been kept out of a Brahmin temple. When Assamese people move to Delhi or Bengaluru, one of the first things they build is a namghar.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The building that holds an Assamese village together.
spotlights.memory_hook: A temple without a god in it, where the village also holds its meetings.

spotlights.name: Kamakhya Temple
spotlights.when: Rebuilt 1565 by the Koch king Nara Narayan
spotlights.spot_it: Beehive-shaped domes over red-and-ochre walls on a hilltop, long queues and goats tied in the courtyard.
spotlights.story_md: Kamakhya is one of the Shakti Peethas, where by legend parts of the goddess Sati's body fell. Here it was the yoni. There is no image inside: in a dark cave below the sanctum, a cleft in the rock is kept wet by an underground spring and covered with flowers and red cloth. The present temple was rebuilt in 1565 by the Koch king Nara Narayan and his brother Chilarai. Its domes are a hybrid style sometimes called Nilachal type. It remains a centre of Tantric worship, and animal sacrifice continues.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One of the most visited and most powerful goddess shrines in India.
spotlights.memory_hook: The goddess has no statue: just a wet stone in a cave on a hill.

spotlights.name: Ambubachi Mela
spotlights.spot_it: Huge crowds and ash-smeared sadhus camped on Nilachal hill around a temple with closed doors.
spotlights.story_md: Once a year, in June, the goddess is believed to menstruate. For three days the temple doors close, farming stops in traditional households, and no one ploughs or plants. On the fourth day the doors reopen and pilgrims receive pieces of red cloth said to be soaked in her flow. Lakhs of pilgrims and Tantric sadhus come for the mela, which is one of the largest gatherings in north-east India. It turns a subject that is taboo in much of India into a festival of fertility.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A rare public celebration of menstruation as sacred.
spotlights.memory_hook: For three days in June, the goddess rests and the farms stop.

spotlights.name: Hajo, three faiths on one hill
spotlights.spot_it: A stone temple with elephant carvings round its base on one hillock, and a white mosque with a dome on another.
spotlights.story_md: Hajo is a small town 24 km from Guwahati with an unusual reputation. Its Hayagriva Madhava temple is a Vishnu shrine, and some Buddhists, especially from Bhutan, believe the Buddha attained nirvana here, a claim historians do not accept but pilgrims act on. On a nearby hill stands the Poa Mecca mosque, built in 1657 by Lutfullah Shirazi around the tomb of the Sufi saint Pir Giasuddin Auliya. Its name means a quarter of Mecca: tradition says praying here earns a quarter of the merit of the Hajj. Hajo is also known for its bell metal and brass work.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A living example of Assam's layered religious geography.
spotlights.memory_hook: In Hajo you can visit a Vishnu temple, a Buddhist legend and a quarter of Mecca before lunch.

compare.difference: Poa Mecca is the hilltop mosque; Hayagriva Madhava is the stone Vishnu temple.

spotlights.name: Azan Fakir and the zikir songs
spotlights.spot_it: A dargah on the Brahmaputra floodplain near Sivasagar; the songs are sung in Assamese, in a style close to Vaishnava devotional music.
spotlights.story_md: Shah Miran, remembered as Azan Fakir because he gave the call to prayer, came to Ahom Assam in the 17th century, by tradition from Baghdad. He learned Assamese and composed zikir and zari songs in it, mixing Sufi ideas with the tunes and imagery of Sankardev's tradition. Tradition says an Ahom king had him blinded on a false charge and later repented and gave him land. His dargah at Saraguri Chapori draws Hindus and Muslims, and zikir is still taught in schools as Assamese literature.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Proof that Assamese Islam has its own voice and its own songs.
spotlights.memory_hook: A Sufi from Baghdad wrote Assamese songs that Hindus still sing.

sections.title: Dance, music, theatre
sections.intro_md:
Assam's performing arts come from three sources: the monasteries, the fields and the tea gardens. From the satras come Sattriya dance, borgeet songs and Bhaona theatre, all created or shaped by Sankardev in the 1500s. From the fields comes Bihu, a spring dance about youth, courtship and planting. From the many peoples of Assam come Bagurumba of the Bodo, Jhumur of the tea-garden Adivasi, the Mising Gumrag and many more.

The instruments are worth learning by sight: the dhol (barrel drum played with a stick and a palm), the pepa (a pipe made of buffalo horn), the gogona (a bamboo jaw harp), the khol (a clay drum used in the satras), the bortaal (big cymbals) and the Bodo serja (a bowed fiddle). Recently the state has turned dance into mass spectacle: 11,304 Bihu dancers in 2023, about 8,000 Jhumur dancers in 2025, about 10,000 Bagurumba dancers in January 2026.

rows.Sattriya: White or cream pat silk, turban for men
rows.Bihu: Muga mekhela chador, red; men in dhoti and gamosa

spotlights.name: Sattriya

where.label: Satras of Majuli and Guwahati stages

spotlights.when: Created in the 16th century; classical since 2000
spotlights.spot_it: Dancers in white or cream silk with flared skirts and tall headdresses, rounded arm movements, accompanied by the khol drum and cymbals.
spotlights.story_md: For about 450 years Sattriya was danced only inside the satras, by celibate male monks, as part of daily worship and plays about Krishna. Men danced the women's roles too. From the 1950s it moved onto public stages, women began to learn it, and on 15 November 2000 the Sangeet Natak Akademi recognised it as one of India's classical dances. It is the only one of them that was kept alive in monasteries rather than temples or courts. Look for the deep, square stance and arms that make circles rather than straight lines.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Assam's classical dance, still taught in the monasteries where it began.
spotlights.memory_hook: A dance kept by monks for 450 years before the world saw it.

compare.difference: Sattriya is slow and devotional with the khol drum; Bihu is fast and flirtatious with the dhol and pepa.

spotlights.name: Bihu dance
spotlights.spot_it: Women in red-bordered muga mekhela chador, hair in a bun with orchids (kopou phul), hands on hips, quick hip flicks; men with dhol and pepa.
spotlights.story_md: Bihu dance was once performed in the open, under trees and in fields, as young people celebrated spring and looked for partners. The songs, bihu geet, are openly romantic and sometimes cheeky. Elite Assamese families once looked down on it; by the 1960s it had become the emblem of the whole state. On 13 April 2023 in Guwahati, 11,304 dancers and 2,548 drummers set Guinness World Records for the largest Bihu dance and the largest performance of the dhol. The orchid in the dancers' hair, kopou, flowers exactly in Bohag, the Bihu month.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The dance every Assamese child knows, and the state's best-known image.
spotlights.memory_hook: Red muga, a kopou orchid in the hair, and a buffalo-horn pipe calling the spring.

spotlights.name: Bhaona (Ankiya Naat)
spotlights.spot_it: An all-night play in a namghar: actors in bright costumes and giant masks of demons and birds, a narrator in white who never leaves the stage.
spotlights.story_md: Bhaona is the performance of Ankiya Naat, the one-act plays Sankardev and Madhavdev wrote about Krishna and Rama. The Sutradhar, a narrator-dancer in white, opens the play, explains it, sings and stays on stage throughout. Demons, Garuda and Narasimha wear huge masks made in the satras. Dialogue is in Brajavali, a literary mix of Assamese and Maithili. A village bhaona can run all night, lit once by oil lamps, and the entrance of the demon is the moment children wait for.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A 500-year-old theatre form still performed by ordinary villagers.
spotlights.memory_hook: The narrator never leaves, and the demon is the star.

spotlights.name: Bagurumba, the butterfly dance
spotlights.spot_it: Lines of Bodo women in yellow-and-green or red dokhona, spreading long scarves (aronai) like wings, moving slowly and softly.
spotlights.story_md: Bagurumba is the signature dance of the Bodo people, usually performed by women at Bwisagu, the Bodo new year in April. Dancers stretch their scarves and move like butterflies, birds or the wind through crops. The music comes from the serja (a bowed string instrument), the sifung (a long bamboo flute) and the kham drum. On 17 January 2026 about 10,000 dancers performed it together at Sarusajai stadium in Guwahati, with the prime minister watching.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The cultural emblem of the Bodo, Assam's largest plains tribe.
spotlights.memory_hook: Ten thousand Bodo women turned a stadium into a field of butterflies.

spotlights.name: Jhumur of the tea gardens
spotlights.spot_it: Women in a line with arms linked at the waist, swaying in step, men with the madal drum and flute, often in tea-garden settings.
spotlights.story_md: Jhumur came to Assam with the Adivasi workers brought from Jharkhand, Odisha and Chhattisgarh to the tea gardens from the 1840s. The songs, in Sadri and other languages, are about work, love, migration and homesickness. Women dance in tight lines with linked arms while men play the madal. On 24 February 2025 about 8,000 performers danced Jhumoir Binandini in Guwahati to mark 200 years of Assam tea. Critics noted that the tea communities still ask for Scheduled Tribe status and better wages.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The voice of the people who built Assam's tea industry.
spotlights.memory_hook: The tea bush came from Assam; the song came with the pickers.

sections.title: Silk, cotton, bamboo and bell metal
sections.intro_md:
In 1921 Gandhi visited Assam and wrote that every Assamese woman is a born weaver. It was close to true: a loom under the house was once part of almost every home, and a girl's weaving was part of her dowry. Assam is often described as the only state that produces all four commercial silks: muga, eri, pat (mulberry) and a little tasar. Sualkuchi, a weaving town on the Brahmaputra, is often called the Manchester of the East.

The other materials are bamboo and cane, which build houses, baskets, fish traps and the japi hat, and bell metal, the copper and tin alloy beaten into plates, bowls and the xorai offering stand in Sarthebari and Hajo. Many of these now carry Geographical Indication tags. The Majuli masks, Sarthebari metal craft, Asharikandi terracotta and the japi were among a batch of Assam GIs announced in 2024.

spotlights.name: Muga silk
spotlights.spot_it: Natural golden-yellow silk with a glossy sheen, never dyed, usually woven with red or white motifs.
spotlights.story_md: Muga is the golden silk of Assam, made by the caterpillar Antheraea assamensis, which is found almost nowhere else on Earth. The worms are raised outdoors on som and soalu trees, and farmers guard them from birds and wasps. The thread is naturally gold and is said to grow brighter with every wash. It is tough enough that a muga mekhela is handed from mother to daughter. Under the Ahoms it was associated with royalty and nobility. A Muga mekhela chador can cost from tens of thousands of rupees upward.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A silk that exists because of one moth that lives almost only in Assam.
spotlights.memory_hook: Gold that grows on trees, spun by a worm, brighter after every wash.

spotlights.name: Eri silk
spotlights.spot_it: Matt, soft, slightly woolly silk in off-white or brick red, woven into warm shawls (eri chador) for winter.
spotlights.story_md: Eri comes from Samia ricini, a silkworm that eats castor leaves. Its cocoon is open at one end, so the moth can leave before the silk is spun. That is why eri is sold as peace silk or ahimsa silk, and why Jain and Buddhist monks wear it. The thread is spun like cotton or wool rather than reeled, which gives it a matt texture and makes it warm. Bodo, Karbi and other communities rear eri at home, and many also eat the pupae, fried, as a delicacy.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The one silk you can make without killing the insect.
spotlights.memory_hook: The peace silk: the moth walks out, then the thread is spun.

spotlights.name: Mekhela chador
spotlights.spot_it: A two-piece dress: a cylindrical pleated lower cloth (mekhela) and a long wrap (chador) tucked at the waist and draped over the shoulder.
spotlights.story_md: The mekhela chador is Assam's signature dress for women, and it is not a sari. The mekhela is a stitched tube of cloth, pleated in front and tucked at the waist. The chador is a separate length wrapped over it and thrown over the left shoulder. An older third piece, the riha, is now worn mostly at weddings. Sets come in muga for weddings and Bihu, pat for festivals and cotton for daily life, woven with motifs of flowers, birds, the kinkhap and the jaapi. Schoolgirls, newsreaders and ministers wear it, and it is Assam's commonest gift for a bride.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The clearest visual sign that a woman is dressed the Assamese way.
spotlights.memory_hook: Not a sari: a tube, a wrap and a shoulder.

spotlights.name: Gamosa
spotlights.spot_it: A white cotton rectangle with a red woven border and red motifs at the ends, draped around the neck of an honoured guest.
spotlights.story_md: The gamosa is a towel, a scarf, a flag and a greeting. Literally it means 'something to wipe the body', yet it is used to welcome guests, to cover the scripture in the namghar, as a Bihu gift (bihuwan) and as a waist-band for Bihu dancers and farmers. Politicians wear it like a stole. During the Assam Movement it became a protest symbol. Every official visitor to Assam gets one placed around the neck with a bow. It received a GI tag in 2022.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The single object that most clearly says Assam.
spotlights.memory_hook: A towel you dry yourself with and give to a prime minister.

spotlights.name: Japi
spotlights.spot_it: A wide conical hat of bamboo and dried tokou palm leaves, plain for farmers or decorated with red and black cloth and mirrors for ceremony.
spotlights.story_md: The japi began as a farmer's sun and rain hat, broad enough to keep off the monsoon in the paddy field. Under the Ahoms richly decorated japis marked rank and were given as honours. Today plain japis still work in fields, while ornamented ones hang on walls, welcome guests at events and open Bihu stages. The frame is split bamboo, the cover is tokou (Livistona) palm leaf, and the best ones are made around Nalbari.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A working hat that became a state emblem.
spotlights.memory_hook: A field umbrella on your head, then a crown for guests.

spotlights.name: Xorai and Sarthebari bell metal
spotlights.spot_it: A footed tray with a domed lid, in gleaming bell metal or brass, sometimes topped with a small bird; holds betel nut and leaf for guests.
spotlights.story_md: The xorai is a raised offering tray, made of bell metal (kanh, an alloy of copper and tin) or brass. It holds tamul-paan for guests, offerings in the namghar, and the gamosa presented to an honoured visitor. Sarthebari in Barpeta district is the bell-metal town, where families beat plates, bowls (bati), water vessels (lota) and xorais by hand. Bell metal rings when struck and was believed to be healthy to eat from. A xorai with a gamosa on top is the standard Assamese honour.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The object at the centre of Assamese hospitality.
spotlights.memory_hook: A gamosa on a xorai: Assam's red carpet.

spotlights.name: Majuli masks (mukha)
spotlights.spot_it: Large painted faces of demons, birds and gods, with bulging eyes and fangs, some big enough to cover the whole body.
spotlights.story_md: The masks of Bhaona are made in the satras of Majuli, above all at Samaguri Satra. The maker builds a frame of split bamboo, covers it with cloth dipped in clay and cow dung, sculpts the face, then paints it with natural colours. There are three types: face masks, larger masks that cover the head, and giant ones that need a performer inside and sometimes movable jaws and eyes. Craftsmen today also make them for collectors and museums, and the tradition has spread to Ravana masks for Ramlila elsewhere.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A living theatre craft that turned into a celebrated art form.
spotlights.memory_hook: Bamboo, clay and cow dung make a demon whose jaw moves.

sections.title: Tea, khar and a pepper that held a world record
sections.intro_md:
Assamese food is light, sour, bitter and herby rather than heavy or sweet. A traditional meal starts with something alkaline, **khar**, and ends with something sour, **tenga**. In between come rice, dal, greens, fish from the rivers and ponds, duck, pigeon, pork among many communities, and fermented bamboo shoot. Spices are used lightly: mustard oil, ginger, garlic, the fruit of the outenga (elephant apple) and a few king chillies, the bhut jolokia, to set the table on fire.

Rice is the centre. Assam grows hundreds of varieties, including **joha**, a small fragrant grain, and **komal saul**, a rice you do not have to cook. Rice beer is part of the culture of many communities: xaaj pani of the Ahoms, apong of the Mising, zou of the Bodo, judima of the Dimasa, which in 2021 became the first rice wine in the north-east to get a GI tag.

And then there is tea. Assam grows its own variety of the plant, makes about half of India's tea, and gave the word 'Assam' to breakfast tables around the world.

spotlights.name: Assam tea
spotlights.spot_it: Endless clipped bushes at waist height under shade trees, women plucking 'two leaves and a bud' into baskets on their backs; in the cup, a dark, malty brew.
spotlights.story_md: In 1823 the Scottish trader Robert Bruce was shown wild tea growing in upper Assam by the Singpho chief Bisa Gam. The Singpho had long drunk it. China held the world's tea monopoly, so the British were eager, but botanists in Calcutta first insisted it was not real tea. It was: a large-leaved local variety now called Camellia sinensis var. assamica. Maniram Dewan, an Assamese noble, guided the early planters and became the first Indian to run his own garden; the British hanged him for joining the 1857 revolt. The first Assam tea sold in London in 1839. In 2025 Assam produced about 688 million kg, roughly half of India's tea. Its strong, malty taste is the base of most 'English breakfast' blends.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Assam's biggest industry and the reason for its colonial history.
spotlights.memory_hook: The British went to China for tea and found it growing wild in Assam.

spotlights.name: Khar
spotlights.spot_it: A pale, slightly cloudy curry of raw papaya or greens with pulses, served first in the meal, in a small bowl.
spotlights.story_md: Khar is both an ingredient and a dish. The ingredient is a liquid alkali: dried peels of a local banana (bhim kol) are burned, and water is filtered through the ash. The dish is usually raw papaya, pulses or greens cooked with a little of this khar, mustard oil and little else. It is eaten at the start of the meal and is believed to help digestion. Khar is so central that Assamese people tease themselves as 'khar-khowa Axomiya', the khar-eating Assamese.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The taste that defines Assamese food, and a word Assamese use about themselves.
spotlights.memory_hook: Burn a banana peel, drink the ash water: that is khar.

spotlights.name: Masor tenga
spotlights.spot_it: A thin, bright orange-red fish curry with tomato, often with pieces of rohu and a squeeze of lemon on top.
spotlights.story_md: Masor tenga means sour fish. It is a light curry of river fish, rohu or the small bony fish of the wetlands, made sour with tomato, outenga (elephant apple), kaji nemu lemons or the leaves of the tenga mora plant. There is very little spice and almost no oil. It closes the meal and is eaten most in summer as a cooler. Restaurants in Guwahati serve it as the state's signature dish, usually after khar and before the sweet.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The everyday dish most Assamese people would call home food.
spotlights.memory_hook: Khar to start, tenga to finish.

spotlights.name: Bhut jolokia
spotlights.spot_it: Wrinkled, pointed red or orange chillies, thin-skinned, about 6 to 8 cm long; a little is mixed into pickles and chutneys.
spotlights.story_md: In 2007 Guinness World Records named the bhut jolokia, or ghost pepper, the hottest chilli in the world, at over 1,000,000 Scoville heat units, about 200 times a jalapeno at its hottest. It held the title until 2011, when hybrids from Trinidad and later the Carolina Reaper beat it. In Assam and Nagaland it is eaten carefully, usually as a sliver in pickle or a rubbed-in note in pork and fish. The Indian defence research agency DRDO has tested it in chilli grenades and pepper spray, and farmers have smeared it on fences to keep wild elephants away.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A local chilli that became a global spice-challenge legend.
spotlights.memory_hook: Hot enough for a world record, a grenade and an elephant fence.

spotlights.name: Komal saul, the rice you do not cook
spotlights.spot_it: Cooked-looking soft white rice in a bowl of cold water with curd, jaggery and banana.
spotlights.story_md: Komal saul, from a sticky rice called bao or boka, is parboiled and dried after harvest. Afterwards it softens in cold water in about 30 to 45 minutes, with no fire at all. It is eaten for breakfast or as a snack with curd, jaggery, milk or bananas. Assamese tradition says the Ahom army carried it on campaign because it needed no cooking. Boka chaul received a GI tag in 2018, and it is still packed for journeys and floods.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A rice that turns any bowl of water into a meal.
spotlights.memory_hook: Add cold water, wait half an hour, eat: rice without fire.

spotlights.name: Rice beer: xaaj pani, apong, zou, judima
spotlights.spot_it: A milky white or grey-brown drink served in bamboo tubes, brass bowls or banana-leaf cups, poured from a gourd or pot.
spotlights.story_md: For many Assamese communities rice beer is food, offering and hospitality. The Ahom make xaaj pani, the Mising make apong (white, or black with burnt rice husk ash), the Bodo make zou, the Dimasa make judima. The starter is a dried cake of rice and herbs, sometimes with dozens of plants, that each family guards. Rice beer is offered to ancestors at Me-Dam-Me-Phi and to guests at Mising festivals. Judima became the first rice wine in the north-east to get a GI tag, in 2021.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A drink at the centre of tribal ritual and hospitality.
spotlights.memory_hook: Every family's yeast cake is a secret recipe of rice and forest herbs.

sections.title: Three Bihus and a year of festivals
sections.intro_md:
Assam has three Bihus, each tied to a stage of the rice year. **Rongali** or Bohag Bihu, in mid-April, is the new year and the sowing season: cattle are bathed and fed on the first day (Goru Bihu), people visit and give gamosas on the second (Manuh Bihu), and for weeks troupes of husori singers go door to door. **Kongali** or Kati Bihu, in October, is the hungry Bihu: granaries are nearly empty, and people light lamps at the foot of the tulsi plant and in the fields. **Bhogali** or Magh Bihu, in mid-January, is the harvest feast, with a night of eating called uruka and bonfires at dawn.

Around these sit the festivals of Assam's many peoples, from the Mising sowing festival Ali-Aye-Ligang in February, with its circling Gumrag dance, to the Ahom ancestor rites of Me-Dam-Me-Phi on 31 January, a barter fair on a lake shore, Bwisagu of the Bodo, Durga Puja in the Barak Valley, and the Raas festival on Majuli each November, where monks stage Krishna's life for several nights.

data.name: Magh Bihu, Jonbeel Mela, Me-Dam-Me-Phi (31 Jan)
Asom Divas (2 Dec), Hornbill season next door

spotlights.name: Magh Bihu: uruka and the meji
spotlights.spot_it: A tall tower of firewood, bamboo and hay (the meji) burning at dawn on a harvested paddy field; a hut of straw (bhelaghar) nearby.
spotlights.story_md: On the night before Magh Bihu, young men build a bhelaghar, a temporary hut of straw and bamboo, and a meji, a tall stack of wood, in the harvested fields. They cook and feast all night: this is uruka, with fish, duck, pork or mutton, and pitha rice cakes. Communities hold group fishing in wetlands that day. Before sunrise the meji is set alight, people offer pitha and betel nut to the fire, and later the bhelaghar is burned too. Ash and charred bits are thrown on fruit trees for a good crop.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The harvest festival, and the most food-centred day of the Assamese year.
spotlights.memory_hook: Build a hut of straw, feast all night, burn it at dawn.

spotlights.name: Jonbeel Mela, the barter fair
spotlights.when: Three days in January, after Magh Bihu
spotlights.spot_it: Rows of hill people with ginger, turmeric and chillies facing plains people with dried fish and rice cakes, swapping goods without money.
spotlights.story_md: Every January, near Jagiroad in Morigaon district, Tiwa, Karbi, Khasi and Jaintia people come down from the hills to meet plains people at a lake called Jonbeel, the moon-shaped lake. For three days they trade by barter: hill turmeric, ginger, chillies and taro for plains fish, rice cakes and sweets. The Tiwa king, the Gobha Raja, attends with his court and collects a token tribute. Tradition traces the fair to the 15th century. It is one of the few large barter markets left in India, a few kilometres from the site of Tata's new chip plant.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A medieval barter economy still alive next to India's newest industry.
spotlights.memory_hook: A king, a moon-shaped lake and a market with no money.

sections.title: How people live
sections.intro_md:
Hospitality in Assam is ritualised. A guest is offered tamul-paan, areca nut and betel leaf, often on a xorai, and on formal occasions a gamosa. Invitations to weddings and funerals were traditionally made by handing over tamul-paan in person. Shoes come off before entering a home or namghar.

Rice is the measure of a meal, and many families still eat from bell-metal plates. Houses in the villages are often built of bamboo, with a courtyard, a pond for fish and a granary on stilts. Among the river peoples, the Mising especially, whole houses stand on stilts above the flood line.

Some numbers help. Assam's NFHS-5 survey (2019 to 2021) found 31.8% of women aged 20 to 24 married before 18, well above the national 23.3%. The state has since run large campaigns against child marriage, including mass arrests in 2023. Women have long worked in the fields, the looms and the tea gardens, where they do most of the plucking.

spotlights.name: Tamul-paan
spotlights.spot_it: Quartered raw or fermented areca nut with a folded betel leaf and a dab of lime, offered on a bell-metal xorai or plate.
spotlights.story_md: In Assam, offering tamul-paan is how you say welcome, thank you, sorry or please come. Unlike the sweet paan of north India, Assamese tamul is often raw or fermented: nuts are buried in pits for months until they soften and turn pungent, and the result can make a first-timer sweat and feel light-headed. Tamul-paan is offered to guests, to elders at Bihu, to the fire at Magh Bihu and to the gods. A betel-nut tree grows beside most rural homes. Doctors now warn that areca nut is a carcinogen, and north-east India has some of the country's highest rates of mouth and throat cancer.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The everyday gesture of Assamese respect, with a real health cost.
spotlights.memory_hook: Welcome, sorry and please, all said with a fermented nut.

spotlights.name: Mising stilt house (chang ghar)

where.label: Majuli and the riverbanks of upper Assam

spotlights.spot_it: A long bamboo house raised on wooden or bamboo posts about 1.5 to 2 metres above the ground, with a thatched roof and a ladder.
spotlights.story_md: The Mising live closer to the Brahmaputra than almost anyone, so they build up. A chang ghar is a long bamboo house on stilts, with the floor high enough that ordinary floods pass underneath. Pigs and poultry live below, and a hearth burns in the middle of the house on a clay base, with fish and meat drying above it. One long house can hold an extended family. Architects now study these houses as models for flood-resilient building.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A practical, low-cost answer to a river that floods every year.
spotlights.memory_hook: When the river comes, the Mising house simply stands on tiptoe.

sections.title: People to know
sections.intro_md: Assam's best-known people are mostly artists and athletes. Two singers in particular, Bhupen Hazarika and Zubeen Garg, became something closer to national voices: they sang about the Brahmaputra, the hills, poverty and unity, and their deaths, in 2011 and 2025, brought the state to a halt. Before them, Jyoti Prasad Agarwala built a film studio in a tea garden and made the first Assamese film. In sport, two young women from small villages, the sprinter Hima Das and the boxer Lovlina Borgohain, Olympic bronze medallist in 2021, put Assam on the world stage within three years.

spotlights.name: Bhupen Hazarika
spotlights.spot_it: A big man in a dark Nehru cap and kurta, gentle smile, singing with a deep baritone; statues of him stand in Guwahati and Jorhat.
spotlights.story_md: Bhupen Hazarika sang his first recorded song at about 12, earned a PhD in mass communication at Columbia University in New York in 1952, and met the singer Paul Robeson there. Robeson's 'Ol' Man River' became 'Bistirno Parore', a song asking the Brahmaputra why it flows on in silence while people suffer; in Hindi it is 'Ganga behti ho kyun'. He scored films in Assamese, Bengali and Hindi, including 'Dil hoom hoom kare' for Rudaali (1993). He won the Dadasaheb Phalke Award in 1992 and the Bharat Ratna, after his death, in 2019. India's longest river bridge when it opened, the Dhola-Sadiya, is named after him.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The voice of 20th-century Assam, and a bridge-builder between its peoples.
spotlights.memory_hook: He took an American river song and gave it to the Brahmaputra.

spotlights.name: Jyoti Prasad Agarwala and Joymoti
spotlights.spot_it: Black-and-white still of a woman tied to a post, from the 1935 film; or a portrait of a young man with a parted moustache.
spotlights.story_md: Jyoti Prasad Agarwala, a playwright, poet and composer from a Marwari-origin family of Tezpur, studied in Edinburgh and visited film studios in Germany. Back in Assam he set up a makeshift studio, Chitraban, at the Bholaguri tea estate and in 1935 released Joymoti, the first Assamese film, about an Ahom princess tortured to death for refusing to betray her husband. It flopped. Most of the film was later lost, and only fragments survive. Assam marks his death anniversary, 17 January, as Silpi Divas, Artists' Day. He is remembered as Rupkonwar, the prince of beauty.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The founder of Assamese cinema.
spotlights.memory_hook: A studio in a tea garden made Assam's first film, and the film vanished.

spotlights.name: Zubeen Garg
spotlights.spot_it: Long hair, a bandana or cap, a wide grin, often on stage with a guitar; after September 2025 his face covers walls across Assam.
spotlights.story_md: Zubeen Garg was born in Tura, Meghalaya, in 1972, sang in Assamese, Bengali, Hindi and dozens of other languages, and became famous across India for 'Ya Ali' from Gangster (2006). In Assam he was more than a pop star: a rebel who mocked politicians, backed local causes and sang Bihu songs that every teenager knew. He died on 19 September 2025 in Singapore, where he had gone for a festival; a death certificate gave drowning as the cause. His body's 30 km journey from the airport took about seven hours through crowds. He was cremated with state honours at Kamarkuchi on 23 September, and the state observed three days of mourning. Investigations into the circumstances continued in 2026.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The most loved Assamese singer of his generation, and a grief that united the state.
spotlights.memory_hook: A city walked his coffin home and sang his songs the whole way.

spotlights.name: Hima Das, the Dhing Express
spotlights.spot_it: A young sprinter with a ponytail draped in the Indian flag, or in a 400 m race on a blue track.
spotlights.story_md: Hima Das grew up in a rice-farming family in Dhing, Nagaon, playing football with boys in the paddy fields. A coach spotted her speed in 2017. A year later, on 12 July 2018 in Tampere, Finland, she won the 400 m at the World U20 Championships in 51.46 seconds, the first Indian to win a world-level gold in a track event. The clip of her crying through the anthem went viral. She was made a deputy superintendent of police in Assam and won the Arjuna Award.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Proof that a world-class sprinter can come out of a paddy field in Nagaon.
spotlights.memory_hook: From muddy football in the rice fields to the anthem in Finland in a year.

sections.title: Places to go
sections.intro_md:
A first trip to Assam usually runs along the river. **Guwahati** is the gateway: Kamakhya on Nilachal hill, the river cruise and Umananda island, the Assam State Museum, and the Srimanta Sankardev Kalakshetra arts complex. **Pobitora**, an hour away, has the densest rhino population in the world in a tiny sanctuary. East along the highway is **Kaziranga** (open roughly November to April), then **Jorhat** for tea estates and the gibbons of Hoollongapar, and the ferry to **Majuli** for the satras and masks. **Sivasagar** holds the Ahom monuments: Rang Ghar, Talatal Ghar, Kareng Ghar and the Sivadol, and Charaideo's moidams are close by. In the far east, **Dibrugarh** and **Tinsukia** have tea bungalows, the oil town of Digboi and the Bogibeel bridge. The west has **Manas** and the Bodo heartland, the south the hill town of **Haflong**.

Best time: October to April. Avoid the peak monsoon, June to September, when floods close roads and parks.

spotlights.name: Sivadol, Sivasagar
spotlights.spot_it: A tall, slim spire topped with a gilded dome, beside a large rectangular tank of water, flanked by two smaller temples.
spotlights.story_md: On the bank of the Borpukhuri tank in Sivasagar stands a temple tower about 32 m tall, often described as the tallest Shiva temple in India. It was built in 1734 by Queen Ambika, wife of the Ahom king Siva Singha, along with the Vishnudol and Devidol beside it. The tank itself, about 52 hectares, was dug at the same time and sits higher than the surrounding town. The town's name means the ocean of Shiva. Siva Singha's reign is also remembered because he let his queens rule in his name, after astrologers warned of bad fortune.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The most striking Ahom temple and the centre of the old capital.
spotlights.memory_hook: A queen built Shiva a tower over a man-made ocean.

sections.title: How Assam earns
sections.intro_md:
For most of the last 150 years Assam's economy rested on three things: tea, oil and rice. Tea gives work to lakhs of people across about 800 large estates and many more small growers. Oil was found in the 1860s and 1880s; Assam still pumps a large share of India's onshore crude, and has refineries at Digboi, Guwahati, Numaligarh and Bongaigaon.

Assam was also long cut off. The Brahmaputra was a moat. Bridges have changed that: Saraighat in 1962, Bogibeel and Dhola-Sadiya in the last decade, with more under construction. The state's GSDP was budgeted at about ₹7.4 lakh crore for 2025-26, and the 2026-27 budget projects about ₹8.7 lakh crore. Per capita income has risen fast but remains among the lower states in India: the budget speech put it at ₹1,85,429 for 2025-26.

The new bet is industry. Tata Electronics is building a ₹27,000 crore chip assembly and testing plant at Jagiroad, designed to handle up to 48 million chips a day.

spotlights.name: Digboi refinery
spotlights.spot_it: An old oil town in the forest: a nodding donkey pump, a heritage museum, and the refinery chimneys of Indian Oil.
spotlights.story_md: The story goes that British railway engineers laying track near the Dihing river saw elephants come out of the forest with oily mud on their feet. Drilling began, and in 1889 the Assam Railways and Trading Company struck oil at Digboi. The refinery opened in 1901 and is still working, under Indian Oil, which makes it the oldest operating refinery in Asia and one of the oldest in the world. The famous story that the town is named after an Englishman shouting 'Dig, boy, dig' at his workers has no documentary support and is best treated as a myth.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The start of India's oil industry.
spotlights.memory_hook: Elephants with oily feet led the way to Asia's oldest working refinery.

spotlights.name: Bogibeel Bridge
spotlights.spot_it: A very long, low, two-level steel truss bridge across a wide braided river: road on top, railway below.
spotlights.story_md: Bogibeel is India's longest rail-cum-road bridge, about 4.94 km across the Brahmaputra between Dibrugarh and Dhemaji. Approved in 1997, it took more than 20 years to build and opened on 25 December 2018. Before it, crossing from one bank to the other in upper Assam could take a day by ferry and road. It also matters for defence, carrying heavy army equipment towards the Arunachal border with China. The deck is designed to carry tanks.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It joined the two banks of upper Assam for the first time.
spotlights.memory_hook: A day's ferry journey became a ten-minute drive.

sections.title: Myths and facts
sections.intro_md: Assam attracts myths, some told by outsiders and some by Assamese people about themselves. Here are the most common, checked against evidence. The short version: the birds of Jatinga are not suicidal, Digboi is not named after a British foreman, the Rang Ghar is very old but 'Asia's oldest amphitheatre' is a slogan, and the north-east is not all one culture. Assam's own peoples differ from each other as much as Kerala differs from Punjab.

data.truth: Fog, wind and village lights confuse night-flying, mostly young birds.

data.claim: Digboi is named after 'Dig, boy, dig'
data.truth: A popular story with no documentary support; the place name predates the oil wells.

data.claim: Majuli is the world's largest river island
data.truth: Guinness listed it in 2016; it is shrinking, and Brazil's Bananal island is far larger if counted as a river island.

data.claim: Rang Ghar is Asia's oldest amphitheatre
data.truth: It dates to about 1746; older viewing structures exist elsewhere in Asia.

data.claim: Assam tea was introduced from China
data.truth: Assam's plant is a native variety, assamica, used by the Singpho before the British. Chinese seed was also planted early on.
The gold is the natural colour of the fibre.

data.claim: Assamese is a dialect of Bengali
data.truth: It is a separate Eastern Indo-Aryan language, declared classical in 2024.
The story comes from later chronicles and folk memory; treat as legend.

sections.title: What is happening now
sections.intro_md:
**September 2025.** Zubeen Garg dies in Singapore on 19 September; Assam observes three days of state mourning and crowds line the roads for days. Investigations into his death continue into 2026.

**January 2026.** About 10,000 Bodo dancers perform Bagurumba together at Sarusajai stadium on 17 January, part of a run of state-backed mass cultural shows.

**February 2026.** Tea Board figures show Assam produced about 688 million kg of tea in 2025, roughly half of India's 1,370 million kg.

**May 2026.** The BJP-led NDA wins 102 of 126 seats in the assembly election; the BJP alone wins 82, its first majority on its own in Assam. Himanta Biswa Sarma is sworn in for a second term on 12 May.

**September 2026.** On World Rhino Day the state says Assam holds about 3,260 greater one-horned rhinos, about 80% of the world population, and recorded no known rhino poaching in 2025.

**October 2026.** Tata Electronics begins pilot production at its Jagiroad chip assembly and test plant; a formal inauguration is expected around December 2026 or January 2027.

spotlights.name: Tata semiconductor plant, Jagiroad
spotlights.spot_it: A large new industrial campus off the highway east of Guwahati, built on the land of a closed paper mill.
spotlights.story_md: Jagiroad was once known for a paper mill that shut down. On that land Tata Electronics is building India's first semiconductor unit in the north-east, a ₹27,000 crore OSAT plant: outsourced semiconductor assembly and test. It does not make wafers. It packages and tests chips made elsewhere, using wire bond, flip chip and system-in-package methods, with a designed capacity of up to 48 million chips a day. Qualcomm has signed on for automotive modules. By October 2026 the first clean room was ready and pilot chips were coming off the line.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Assam's biggest bet on an economy beyond tea and oil.
spotlights.memory_hook: A dead paper mill reborn as a chip factory next to a barter fair.

sections.title: Recap
sections.intro_md:
Assam is a river valley: the Brahmaputra made its soil, its floods, its islands and its isolation. On that land the Ahoms built a kingdom that lasted almost 600 years, buried their kings in moidams and beat the Mughals at Saraighat in 1671. Sankardev gave the Assamese a religion without idols, the namghar, the satra, Sattriya dance and Bhaona theatre. The British made it a tea and oil colony and brought the migrations that still shape its politics, from the Assam Accord's 1971 cut-off to the 2019 NRC.

To recognise Assam on sight: a red-bordered gamosa, golden muga silk, a japi hat, a bell-metal xorai with tamul-paan, a one-horned rhino in tall grass, a Bihu dancer with a kopou orchid in her hair. To taste it: khar first, masor tenga last, a cup of strong malty tea. To hear it: the pepa horn, the khol drum and Bhupen Hazarika asking the river why it flows on.

side_dish.title: Why the Brahmaputra braids
side_dish.body_md:
Look at the Brahmaputra from a plane and it does not look like one river. It looks like rope that has frayed: dozens of channels splitting and rejoining around sandbars. Geographers call this a braided river, and the reason is a simple balance between how much sediment a river carries and how much energy it has to move it.

The Brahmaputra drains the eastern Himalaya, some of the youngest, fastest-rising and most earthquake-shaken mountains on Earth. Landslides and heavy monsoon rain feed it enormous amounts of sand and silt. When the river leaves the mountains and reaches the flat Assam valley, its slope drops sharply and it slows down. A slower river can carry less, so it drops sand in its own bed. The bars that form push the water sideways into new channels, which build new bars, and so on.

Two other things make it worse. The 1950 Assam earthquake, magnitude 8.6, threw huge amounts of debris into the rivers and raised parts of the bed. And the banks are loose sand and silt, easy to cut. So the river wanders, eats one bank and builds land on the other. That is why Majuli shrinks, why chars appear and vanish, and why embankments often fail. A braided river is not a broken river. It is doing exactly what physics expects.

offline_task.title: Make masor tenga, Assam's sour fish curry
offline_task.body_md:
**Serves 2. About 30 minutes. Very little spice: the point is sour and fresh.**

**You need**
- 4 pieces of rohu or any firm freshwater fish (or paneer if you do not eat fish)
- 3 ripe tomatoes, chopped
- 1 tablespoon mustard oil, plus a little for frying
- half a teaspoon fenugreek (methi) seeds, or panch phoron
- half a teaspoon turmeric, salt
- 1 or 2 green chillies, slit
- juice of half a lemon, a handful of coriander

**Method**
1. Rub the fish with turmeric and salt. Fry lightly in mustard oil until just golden. Set aside.
2. In the same pan, heat a tablespoon of mustard oil until it smokes, then let it cool for 20 seconds. Add the fenugreek seeds.
3. Add the tomatoes, a pinch of turmeric and salt. Cook until soft, mashing as you go.
4. Pour in about 2 cups of water and bring to a boil. Add the green chillies and the fish. Simmer 5 to 7 minutes.
5. Turn off the heat, add the lemon juice and coriander.

Eat it with plain rice, as the last course of the meal. If you can find outenga (elephant apple) or Assamese kaji nemu lemons, use them instead of tomato or lemon for the real taste. Notice how light it is compared with a north Indian curry.
